lessons.title: Sets and functions
lessons.summary: Set notation and operations, power sets and Cartesian products, injective, surjective and bijective functions, and why infinite sets come in different sizes.
lessons.body:
Almost every structure in computer science is built from two ideas: a **set** (a collection of things) and a **function** (a rule that maps each thing in one set to exactly one thing in another). A simple model treats a type as a set of values and a mathematical relation as a set of tuples. SQL tables can contain duplicate rows, and a hash table usually maps a key through a hash value to a bucket. Getting fluent with the vocabulary pays off everywhere else in this subject.

## Sets

A set is an unordered collection of distinct elements. Curly braces list what is in it, and only membership counts: the order you write the elements in and any repeats make no difference.

```formula
{1, 2, 3} = {3, 1, 2} = {1, 1, 2, 3}
where
{ }: curly braces: the set whose elements are the things listed inside, separated by commas
=: the two sets are equal: they have exactly the same elements
In words: all three ways of writing it describe the same set, the one containing exactly 1, 2 and 3. Changing the order or repeating 1 does not make a new set.
```

Notation you will see constantly:

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| x ∈ A | x is an element of A |
| x ∉ A | x is not an element of A |
| A ⊆ B | every element of A is in B |
| A ⊂ B | A ⊆ B and A ≠ B (proper subset) |
| ∅ | the empty set, {} |
| \|A\| | the cardinality (size) of A |

In this table, ≠ means "is not equal to", and the capital letters A and B stand for any two sets.

For example, with A = {1, 2} and B = {1, 2, 3}:

```formula
1 ∈ A     3 ∉ A
A ⊆ B     A ⊂ B
|A| = 2   |B| = 3
where
A: the example set {1, 2}
B: the example set {1, 2, 3}
∈: is an element of
∉: is not an element of
⊆: is a subset of: every element of the left-hand set is also in the right-hand set (the two may be equal)
⊂: is a proper subset of: a subset that is not equal, so the right-hand set has at least one extra element
| |: vertical bars around a set mean its cardinality: the number of elements it has
In words: 1 is in A but 3 is not; everything in A is also in B, and B has an extra element (3), so A is a proper subset of B; A has 2 elements and B has 3.
```

Sets can be written by listing elements, or with **set-builder notation**, which describes the elements by a rule. It resembles a Python comprehension, but mathematical sets can also be infinite:

```formula
E = { x ∈ ℤ : 0 ≤ x < 10, x mod 2 = 0 }
E = {0, 2, 4, 6, 8}
where
E: the set being defined (the even numbers below 10)
x: a stand-in for each candidate element
ℤ: the integers: …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …
∈: is an element of
{ x ∈ ℤ : … }: set-builder notation: the set of all integers x that make the condition after the colon true. The colon reads "such that"; some books write a vertical bar | instead
≤: is less than or equal to
<: is less than
mod: the remainder after dividing, so x mod 2 = 0 means x is even
In words: E is the set of integers x with 0 ≤ x < 10 that are even, which works out to {0, 2, 4, 6, 8}.
```

The same set in Python, where `%` is the remainder operator:

```python
E = {x for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0}
```

Common number sets: ℕ (natural numbers; whether 0 is included varies by author, so check), ℤ (integers), ℚ (rationals, the fractions of integers) and ℝ (reals, every point on the number line).

> [!warning] Elements versus subsets
> The empty set is a subset of every set, but it is an element of a set only if that set literally lists the empty set inside its braces. The set containing just the empty set has one element; the empty set itself has none.

```formula
∅ ⊆ A   for every A
∅ ∈ {∅}     ∅ ∉ {1, 2}
|{∅}| = 1   |∅| = 0
where
∅: the empty set, the set with no elements, also written {}
A: any set at all
⊆: is a subset of: every element of the left-hand set is in the right-hand set
∈: is an element of
∉: is not an element of
{ }: curly braces: the set of the things listed inside
| |: the cardinality: the number of elements in the set
In words: the empty set is a subset of everything (it has no element that could fail to be in A), but it is only an element of a set that lists it, like {∅}. That set has one element; ∅ has none.
```

## Set operations

These operations build new sets from old ones. The **universe** U is the set of everything under discussion (all users, all integers), which a complement needs so it knows what "not in A" ranges over.

```formula
A ∪ B = { x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B }
A ∩ B = { x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B }
A \ B = { x : x ∈ A and x ∉ B }
A ⊕ B = (A ∪ B) \ (A ∩ B)
Aᶜ = U \ A
where
A, B: any two sets
x: a stand-in for an element
U: the universe: the set of everything under discussion
∪: union: in A or B (or both)
∩: intersection: in both A and B
\: set difference: in A but not in B (some books write A − B)
⊕: symmetric difference: in exactly one of the two sets (some books write A △ B)
ᶜ: complement: everything in the universe U that is not in A
∈: is an element of
∉: is not an element of
{ x : … }: the set of all x that make the condition after the colon true
In words: union keeps anything in either set, intersection keeps what they share, difference keeps A's elements that B lacks, symmetric difference keeps what is in exactly one, and the complement is everything in the universe that is not in A.
```

The picture shows how the three regions of two overlapping sets line up with these operations:

```
   +-------+-------+
   |  A    |    B  |
   | only  | both  |  only
   |  A\B  |  A∩B  |  B\A
   +-------+-------+
```

A worked example, with a universe of the numbers 1 to 6:

```formula
A = {1, 2, 3, 4}   B = {3, 4, 5}
A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
A ∩ B = {3, 4}
A \ B = {1, 2}
A ⊕ B = {1, 2, 5}
Aᶜ = {5, 6}   for U = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}
where
A, B: the two example sets
U: the universe, here the numbers 1 to 6
∪: union: in A or B (or both)
∩: intersection: in both
\: difference: in A but not in B
⊕: symmetric difference: in exactly one of A and B
ᶜ: complement: in the universe but not in A
In words: the union has every number from either set, the intersection only the shared 3 and 4, the difference A's numbers that B lacks, the symmetric difference everything except the shared 3 and 4, and the complement the numbers in U that A misses.
```

Python's built-in set supports union, intersection, difference and symmetric difference; complement needs an explicit universe, `U - a`. They are the bread and butter of practical code (deduplicating, finding common users, permission checks):

```python
a = {1, 2, 3, 4}
b = {3, 4, 5}
a | b   # {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
a & b   # {3, 4}
a - b   # {1, 2}
a ^ b   # {1, 2, 5}
a <= b  # False: is a a subset of b?
```

Two laws worth memorising are **De Morgan's laws**, which mirror the logic versions. They say how a complement passes through a union or an intersection:

```formula
(A ∪ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ
(A ∩ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∪ Bᶜ
where
A, B: any two sets inside a universe U
ᶜ: complement: everything in the universe U that is not in the set
∪: union: in either set
∩: intersection: in both sets
In words: "not in (A or B)" is the same as "not in A and not in B", and "not in (A and B)" is the same as "not in A or not in B". The complement flips union into intersection and back.
```

Check the first law with the example sets from above:

```formula
A = {1, 2, 3, 4}   B = {3, 4, 5}
(A ∪ B)ᶜ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}ᶜ = {6}
Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ = {5, 6} ∩ {1, 2, 6} = {6}
where
A, B: the two example sets, inside the universe U = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}
U: the universe: everything under discussion, here the numbers 1 to 6
ᶜ: complement: the elements of U that are not in the set
∪: union: in either set
∩: intersection: in both sets
In words: only 6 is outside both sets, and computing it either way gives {6}, so the two sides of the law agree.
```

This is the same rewrite you do when you push a `NOT` through an SQL WHERE clause.

## Power sets and Cartesian products

The **power set** P(A) is the set of all subsets of A. Its size is a power of two, because each element is independently either in or out of a subset: two choices, made once per element.

```formula
|P(A)| = 2^n   when |A| = n
A = {a, b, c}
P(A) = { ∅, {a}, {b}, {c}, {a, b},
         {a, c}, {b, c}, {a, b, c} }
|P(A)| = 2^3 = 8
where
A: any finite set; in the example, the set of the three letters a, b and c
a, b, c: the three elements of the example set
P(A): the power set of A: the set whose elements are all the subsets of A
n: the number of elements in A
| |: the cardinality: the number of elements in a set
∅: the empty set, the subset with nothing in it
{ }: the set of the things listed inside
2^n: n copies of 2 multiplied together
In words: a set of n elements has 2^n subsets, counting both the empty set and the whole set. Three elements give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 subsets.
```

That "in or out" view is exactly how programmers enumerate subsets with a **bitmask**: an integer whose binary digits (bits) say which elements are in. Number the elements from 0 upwards; each bit of the mask is 1 when the element with that number is in the subset.

```formula
m = x_0 × 2^0 + x_1 × 2^1 + …
      + x_{n−1} × 2^{n−1}
0 ≤ m ≤ 2^n − 1
{b, c} → m = 0 × 1 + 1 × 2 + 1 × 4 = 6
where
m: the mask: one whole number standing for one subset
x_0, x_1, x_{n−1}: the bits of the mask: bit number i is 1 if element number i is in the subset and 0 if not, for i from 0 up to n − 1
n: the number of elements in the set
2^0, 2^1, 2^{n−1}: powers of 2 (1, 2, 4, …), the place value of each bit
…: and so on, one term for every element
≤: is less than or equal to
→: is encoded as
b, c: in the last line, elements 1 and 2 of {a, b, c} (a is element 0)
In words: every subset of an n-element set corresponds to exactly one whole number from 0 to 2^n − 1. For {a, b, c}, the subset {b, c} is mask 6, binary 110.
```

The loop below visits every mask and decodes it back into a subset:

```python
items = ['a', 'b', 'c']
n = len(items)
for mask in range(1 << n):
    sub = [items[i] for i in range(n)
           if mask >> i & 1]
    print(mask, sub)
```

There are 2ⁿ subsets: about a million for 20 items and about a trillion for 40. Runtime also includes work per subset. The loop above checks n bit positions for each of the 2ⁿ masks:

```formula
T(n) = Θ(n × 2^n)
T(20) ≈ 20 × 1,048,576 ≈ 21,000,000
where
T(n): the number of elementary operations the loop performs for an n-element set
n: the number of elements
Θ( ): grows at the same rate as the expression inside, up to a constant factor (big-Theta notation)
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the work is roughly n bit checks for each of the 2^n subsets, so 20 items already cost about 21 million basic steps before any printing.
```

This assumes each bit check costs one step (a unit-cost model) and ignores the cost of formatting and printing.

The **Cartesian product** A × B is the set of all ordered pairs whose first part comes from A and whose second part comes from B. Every element of A is paired with every element of B, so the sizes multiply:

```formula
A × B = { (a, b) : a ∈ A and b ∈ B }
|A × B| = |A| × |B|
{1, 2} × {x, y}
  = {(1,x), (1,y), (2,x), (2,y)}
|{1, 2} × {x, y}| = 2 × 2 = 4
where
A, B: any two sets
a: an element of A
b: an element of B
x, y: the two elements of the example's second set
×: between sets, the Cartesian product; between numbers, ordinary multiplication
( , ): an ordered pair: order matters, so (1, x) and (x, 1) are different
∈: is an element of
| |: the cardinality: the number of elements
{ : }: the set of all things of the form before the colon that satisfy the condition after it
In words: the Cartesian product pairs every element of A with every element of B, so a 2-element set times a 2-element set gives 4 pairs.
```

A relational table is the same idea with more columns. Each column draws its values from a set of allowed values (its domain), and the table holds a set of rows chosen from all the combinations:

```formula
T ⊆ D_1 × D_2 × … × D_k
where
T: the set of rows in the table, each row a k-tuple (a list of k values in column order)
D_1, D_2, D_k: the domains: the sets of allowed values for column 1, column 2 and column k
k: the number of columns
×: Cartesian product
…: and so on, one factor per column
⊆: is a subset of
In words: a relation (in the database sense) is a set of rows chosen from all possible combinations of column values.
```

Real SQL tables go a little beyond this model: they can hold duplicate rows. An SQL CROSS JOIN combines every input-row occurrence with every occurrence on the other side, retaining duplicate multiplicities.

## Functions

A **function** assigns to every element of its **domain** exactly one element of its **codomain**. Two conditions: every input has an output, and no input has two outputs.

```formula
f : A → B
f(a) ∈ B   for every a ∈ A
where
f: the function's name
A: the domain: the set of allowed inputs
B: the codomain: the set the outputs are declared to lie in
a: any input taken from A
f(a): the single output f gives for input a
→: in "f : A → B", "maps elements of A to elements of B"
∈: is an element of
In words: f takes each element of A and gives back exactly one element of B.
```

The **image** (often called the range) is the set of outputs actually hit:

```formula
f(A) = { f(a) : a ∈ A }
f(A) ⊆ B
where
f(A): the image of f: every output that some input actually produces
f: a function from the set A to the set B
A: the domain, the set of inputs
B: the codomain
a: an input taken from A
f(a): the output for input a
∈: is an element of
⊆: is a subset of
{ : }: the set of all values f(a), one for each a in A
In words: the image collects every output f really produces. It is always inside the codomain and may be smaller.
```

For example, doubling an integer:

```formula
f : ℤ → ℤ,   f(x) = 2 × x
f(ℤ) = {…, −4, −2, 0, 2, 4, …}
where
f: the doubling function
x: an integer input
ℤ: the integers: …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …
f(ℤ): the image of f: every output it actually produces
→: in "f : ℤ → ℤ", f takes integers and its declared codomain is the integers
…: and so on in both directions
In words: doubling hits only the even integers, so the image is smaller than the codomain: 3, for example, is in the codomain but never an output.
```

Three properties matter:

- **Injective** (one-to-one): different inputs give different outputs.
- **Surjective** (onto): every element of the codomain is hit by some input, so the image equals the codomain.
- **Bijective**: both. Every element of the codomain is hit by exactly one input, so f has an **inverse** function that undoes it.

In symbols, for a function f from A to B, the first line is injectivity, the second surjectivity, and the last two describe the inverse of a bijection:

```formula
f(x) = f(y) means x = y
∀ b ∈ B, ∃ a ∈ A such that f(a) = b
f^{−1} : B → A
f^{−1}(f(a)) = a   and   f(f^{−1}(b)) = b
where
f: a function from A to B
A: the domain, the set of inputs
B: the codomain, the set outputs lie in
x, y: any two inputs from A
a: an input from A
b: an element of the codomain B
∀: "for every"
∃: "there exists": at least one such element exists
f^{−1}: the inverse of f, read "f inverse": the function that sends each output back to the one input that produced it. The −1 is a label, not a power: f^{−1} is not 1 / f
∈: is an element of
→: in "f^{−1} : B → A", "maps elements of B to elements of A"
In words: injective means two inputs only share an output if they are the same input; surjective means every b in B is the output of at least one a; when both hold (bijective), every b has exactly one a, so f^{−1} can run f backwards and the round trip in either direction gets you back where you started.
```

```
injective    surjective   bijective
not onto     not 1-to-1
a -> 1       a -> 1       a -> 1
b -> 2       b -> 1       b -> 2
c -> 3       c -> 2       c -> 3
     4
```

In the left column nothing maps to 4, so the map is not onto. In the middle, a and b share 1, so it is not one-to-one. The right column is a perfect pairing.

For finite sets these properties limit the sizes. An injection from A to B can exist only when A is no bigger than B; a surjection only when A is at least as big as B; and a bijection only when they are the same size:

```formula
|A| ≤ |B|
|A| ≥ |B|
|A| = |B|
where
A: the domain, a finite set
B: the codomain, a finite set
| |: the cardinality: the number of elements
≤: is less than or equal to
≥: is greater than or equal to
In words: line 1 must hold for an injection (you cannot send more things to fewer places without two sharing), line 2 for a surjection (you cannot cover more places than you have things), and line 3 for a bijection (a perfect pairing needs equal sizes).
```

The first one is the **pigeonhole principle** in disguise: put 5 pigeons in 4 holes and two pigeons must share.

> [!example] Why hash functions collide
> Standard SHA-256 accepts messages shorter than 2⁶⁴ bits and produces one of 2²⁵⁶ outputs. Its finite input domain is still vastly larger than its output space. No function from a larger set to a smaller one can be injective, so collisions must exist. Cryptographic hashes are designed so that *finding* one is infeasible, not so that none exist.

### Composition and inverses

**Composition** chains two functions: apply one, then feed its output to the other.

```formula
(g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x))
f(x) = x + 1,  g(y) = 2 × y
(g ∘ f)(3) = g(4) = 8
where
f: the first function applied, from A to B
g: the second function applied, from B to C
x: an input from the domain A of f
y: an input to g, from the set B
∘: composition, read "after": g ∘ f means "g after f"
In words: g ∘ f runs f first and then g on the result. With f adding 1 and g doubling, 3 becomes 4 and then 8. The order matters: f ∘ g would give 2 × 3 + 1 = 7.
```

Compositions preserve the properties above: two injections compose to an injection, two surjections to a surjection, and two bijections to a bijection.

If g ∘ f is injective, then f must be injective (if f merged two inputs, g could not separate them again). If a stage merges two reachable states that arose from distinct valid inputs, later deterministic stages cannot recover that distinction without additional information. Non-injectivity only on states the pipeline never reaches need not lose information.

### Counting functions

For finite sets, you can count how many functions of each kind exist. Each input chooses an output; for an injection, each choice must avoid the outputs already used.

```formula
N_all = n^m
N_inj = n! / (n − m)!   if m ≤ n
N_inj = 0   if m > n
N_bij = m!   when A = B
where
N_all: the number of functions from A to B
N_inj: the number of injections from A to B
N_bij: the number of bijections from A to itself

A: the domain, with m elements
B: the codomain, with n elements
m: the number of elements in A (the inputs)
n: the number of elements in B (the possible outputs)
n^m: m copies of n multiplied together
!: factorial: k! = k × (k − 1) × … × 2 × 1, with 0! = 1
≤: is less than or equal to
>: is greater than
In words: each of the m inputs freely picks one of n outputs, giving n^m functions; an injection must use a new output each time, giving n × (n − 1) × … for m factors; a bijection from a set to itself is a reordering (permutation), and there are m! of those.
```

A worked example with m = 3 inputs and n = 4 outputs:

```formula
n^m = 4^3 = 64
n! / (n − m)! = 4! / 1! = 4 × 3 × 2 = 24
where
n: the number of possible outputs, here 4
m: the number of inputs, here 3
!: factorial: the product of all whole numbers from 1 up to that number, so 4! = 24 and 1! = 1
In words: from a 3-element set to a 4-element set there are 64 functions, of which 24 never repeat an output.
```

Use the counting convention 0⁰ = 1 for the unique empty-domain function. There are 2⁸ = 256 functions from the 8 bit positions of a byte to {0, 1}: one per byte value.

## Functions in real code

The mathematical idea of a function is stricter than a programming "function". A routine whose result depends on changing hidden state may return different results for the same explicit arguments. Including the relevant state in the mathematical input gives a function again; reading an immutable constant does not itself violate determinism. Pure terminating routines fit the simple total-function model and can be easier to test, memoise and parallelise.

Bijections show up whenever you need a lossless round trip:

- **Serialisation**: `decode(encode(x)) == x` for every valid x is a requirement that `encode` is injective, and `decode` is its inverse on the image.
- **Base64, UTF-8, gzip**: with a fixed encoder configuration and appropriate valid input domain, lossless round trips require injectivity. Ordinary lossy JPEG and MP3 encoding merge distinct inputs; the JPEG family also includes lossless modes.
- **Primary keys**: projecting each row to its primary-key value uniquely identifies that row. A primary key combines uniqueness with non-nullness; a bare UNIQUE constraint can permit multiple nulls depending on the database and configuration.
- **Permutations in shuffles and ciphers**: a block cipher with a fixed key is a bijection on blocks, otherwise decryption would be ambiguous.

## Infinite sets have different sizes

For infinite sets you cannot count elements, so "same size" is defined by pairing them up: two sets have the same cardinality exactly when there is a bijection between them, so their elements pair off one-to-one with nothing left over on either side. This leads to surprises.

A set is **countable** if it is finite or in bijection with ℕ, the natural numbers 0, 1, 2, …: you can list its elements in a sequence that eventually reaches each one. ℤ (the integers) is countable, even though it seems twice as big, because this bijection lists it as 0, 1, −1, 2, −2, …:

```formula
f(n) = (n + 1) / 2   for n = 1, 3, 5, …
f(n) = −n / 2   for n = 0, 2, 4, …
|ℕ| = |ℤ|
where
ℕ: the natural numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, …
ℤ: the integers …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …
f: a bijection from ℕ to ℤ
n: a natural number, the position in the list
f(n): the integer at position n
…: and so on without end
| |: the cardinality: the size of a set
In words: odd positions get the positive integers (1 → 1, 3 → 2, 5 → 3) and even positions get zero and the negatives (0 → 0, 2 → −1, 4 → −2). Every integer appears once and only once, so ℕ and ℤ have the same size.
```

So is ℚ (the fractions), and so is the set of all finite strings over a finite alphabet, which means **the set of all programs is countable**.

**Cantor's diagonal argument** shows that the set of infinite binary sequences (equivalently, the power set of ℕ, or the real numbers) is **not** countable. Suppose you had a complete list of sequences. Build a new sequence d by flipping the i-th bit of the i-th sequence:

```formula
d(i) = 1 − s_i(i)
d(i) ≠ s_i(i)   for every i
where
s_i: the i-th infinite 0/1 sequence in the supposedly complete list (s_1 first, s_2 second, …)
s_i(i): bit number i of sequence s_i: the bits on the diagonal
d: the new sequence being built
d(i): bit number i of d
i: a position, 1, 2, 3, …
≠: is not equal to
In words: d takes the diagonal bit of each listed sequence and flips it (1 − 0 = 1, 1 − 1 = 0), so d disagrees with every listed sequence somewhere and cannot be on the list.
```

```
s1 = 0 1 1 0 1 ...
s2 = 1 1 0 0 0 ...
s3 = 0 0 0 1 1 ...
s4 = 1 0 1 1 0 ...
d  = 1 0 1 0 ...   (flip diagonal)
```

The diagonal bits are 0, 1, 0, 1, so d starts 1, 0, 1, 0. It differs from s1 in position 1, from s2 in position 2, and so on, so it is not on the list, contradicting completeness. More generally, **Cantor's theorem** says every set is strictly smaller than its power set:

```formula
|P(A)| > |A|   for every A
where
A: any set, finite or infinite
P(A): the power set of A, the set of all its subsets
| |: the cardinality: the size of a set
>: is strictly larger than: there is an injection from A into P(A) but no bijection between them
In words: a set always has more subsets than elements. For finite sets this is 2^n > n; for infinite ones it means there is no largest infinity.
```

> [!note] Why CS cares
> Programs are countable but the set of functions from ℕ to {0, 1} (all possible yes/no problems) is not. So almost all problems have no program that solves them. The halting problem, covered in the computability module, is a concrete example built with the same diagonal trick.

## Pitfalls

- **Codomain versus image.** Whether a function is surjective depends on the declared codomain: squaring real numbers hits every non-negative real, but no negative one (see below).
- **Sets are unordered and deduplicated.** Converting a list to a set and back loses order and duplicates. Python sets only hold hashable elements, so use `frozenset` for a set of sets.
- **Off-by-one in power sets.** The count of subsets includes both the empty set and the whole set. "Non-empty subsets" is one fewer (see below).
- **"Function" in code is not always a function.** Changing hidden state can break the same-explicit-input/same-result rule; an output side effect can violate purity even when the returned result is deterministic.

The two numeric pitfalls in symbols:

```formula
f(x) = x^2,   f(ℝ) = [0, ∞)
N_ne = 2^n − 1
N_ne = 2^3 − 1 = 7   for n = 3
where
f: the squaring function, with domain ℝ
x: a real-number input
x^2: x multiplied by itself
ℝ: the real numbers: every point on the number line
f(ℝ): the image of f: every output it actually produces
[0, ∞): the non-negative reals: every real number from 0 upwards, with no upper limit
∞: infinity: the interval goes on without end
N_ne: the number of non-empty subsets
n: the number of elements in the set whose subsets you count
In words: squaring hits exactly the non-negative reals, so it is surjective if its declared codomain is [0, ∞) and not surjective if the codomain is all of ℝ (−1 is never an output). A set of n elements has 2^n subsets, and all but the empty one are non-empty: 7 for a 3-element set.
```

## Key takeaways
- A set is an unordered collection of distinct elements; union, intersection, difference and symmetric difference map to Python's |, &, - and ^; complement needs an explicit universe U, written U - A in Python.
- A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets, and a Cartesian product has as many pairs as the two sizes multiplied; bitmasks identify the 2ⁿ subsets, and listing each subset explicitly costs about n × 2ⁿ elementary operations in total.
- Injective means no collisions, surjective means every output is hit, bijective means both and implies an inverse.
- From a larger finite set to a smaller one no injection exists, which is why hash collisions are unavoidable.
- Countable sets can be listed; Cantor's diagonal argument shows the power set of ℕ cannot, so most problems have no program.

questions.prompt: A feature-flag system has 5 independent boolean flags. Treating the set of flags that are switched on as a subset of the 5 flags, how many distinct configurations are possible?

options.explanation: 10 is "5 choose 2", the number of ways to pick 2 of the 5 flags, so it counts only the configurations with exactly two flags on. The question allows any number of flags on.
25 is 5², which would be right for two independent choices among 5 options. Here there are 5 independent choices between 2 options, which is 2⁵.
Correct. Each flag is independently on or off, so there are 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 2⁵ = 32 subsets, which is the size of the power set of a 5-element set.
31 is 2⁵ − 1, the number of non-empty subsets. The all-off configuration (the empty set) is a valid configuration too.

questions.workedExample:
Each configuration is a subset of the 5 flags, so we want the size of the power set.

1. For each flag there are 2 choices: in the subset (on) or not (off).
2. The choices are independent, so multiply:

```formula
|P(A)| = 2^n
|P(A)| = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2
|P(A)| = 2^5 = 32
where
A: the set of the 5 flags
P(A): the power set of A: the set of all subsets of A, one per configuration
| |: the cardinality: the number of elements in a set
n: the number of flags, here 5
2^n: n copies of 2 multiplied together, one factor of 2 (on or off) per flag
In words: 5 independent on/off choices give 32 configurations, including all off and all on.
```

The bitmask view makes this concrete: the integers 0 to 31 are exactly the 5-bit patterns, one per configuration.

```
00000  all off  (the empty set)
00001  flag 0 on
...
11111  all on
```

options.explanation: That is `a & b`, the intersection. `^` is symmetric difference, which keeps elements in exactly one of the sets.
That is `a - b`, the difference. Symmetric difference also keeps 5, which is in b but not a.
That is `a | b`, the union. Symmetric difference removes the shared elements 3 and 4.
Correct. `^` is symmetric difference: elements in a or b but not both. 3 and 4 are in both, so they are dropped.

questions.workedExample:
Work it out from the definition of symmetric difference: everything in the union except what is in the intersection.

```formula
A ⊕ B = (A ∪ B) \ (A ∩ B)
A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
A ∩ B = {3, 4}
A ⊕ B = {1, 2, 5}
where
A, B: the sets a = {1, 2, 3, 4} and b = {3, 4, 5} from the code
⊕: symmetric difference: in exactly one of the two sets (Python's ^)
∪: union: in either set (Python's |)
∩: intersection: in both sets (Python's &)
\: set difference: in the left set but not the right one (Python's -)
In words: drop the shared elements 3 and 4 from everything, leaving 1, 2 and 5.
```

The same steps in Python:

```python
a | b   # {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
a & b   # {3, 4}
a ^ b   # {1, 2, 5}
```

`sorted` turns the set into a list in ascending order, so the output is `[1, 2, 5]`. Note that `^` on sets is not XOR of numbers; it is the set version of exclusive or.

questions.prompt:
A function f from {1, 2, 3} to {a, b} is defined by:

```formula
f(1) = a   f(2) = b   f(3) = a
where
f: a function with domain {1, 2, 3} (its inputs) and codomain {a, b} (the allowed outputs)
f(1), f(2), f(3): the output f gives for the inputs 1, 2 and 3
a, b: the two elements of the codomain
In words: f sends 1 and 3 to a, and 2 to b.
```

Which description is correct?

options.text: Injective but not surjective
options.explanation: It is not injective: f sends both 1 and 3 to a, so two different inputs share an output.

options.text: Surjective but not injective
options.explanation: Correct. Both a and b are hit, so it is onto. But 1 and 3 both map to a, so it is not one-to-one.

options.text: Bijective
options.explanation: A bijection needs both properties, and it would also need the two sets to be the same size. Here they have 3 and 2 elements.

options.text: Not a function, because a is used twice
options.explanation: A function may send several inputs to the same output. What it cannot do is send one input to two outputs, or leave an input unmapped.

questions.workedExample:
Check each property separately.

```formula
f(1) = a,  f(2) = b
so   f({1,2,3}) = {a, b}
f(1) = f(3)   with 1 ≠ 3
where
f: the function from {1, 2, 3} to {a, b}
f(1), f(2), f(3): the outputs for inputs 1, 2 and 3
f({1,2,3}): the image: the set of outputs actually produced
a, b: the elements of the codomain {a, b}
≠: is not equal to
In words: both a and b are produced, so f is surjective; two different inputs (1 and 3) share the output a, so f is not injective.
```

1. **Surjective?** The image is the whole codomain {a, b}. Yes.
2. **Injective?** 1 and 3 collide. No.
3. **Bijective?** Needs both, so no.

A quicker sanity check: from a 3-element set to a 2-element set no injection can exist (pigeonhole), so options claiming injectivity are ruled out before you even look at the mapping.

questions.prompt: A set A has 3 elements and a set B has 4. How many functions from A to B are there, and how many of them are injective?

options.text: 64 functions, 24 injective
options.explanation: Correct. Each of the 3 inputs picks any of 4 outputs: 4³ = 64. For an injection the choices must differ: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24.

options.text: 81 functions, 24 injective
options.explanation: 81 is 3⁴, which counts functions from B to A (4 inputs, 3 choices each). The exponent is the size of the domain.

options.text: 12 functions, 4 injective
options.explanation: 12 is 3 × 4, the number of ordered pairs (the size of the Cartesian product of A and B). A function is a choice of one output per input, not a single pair.

options.text: 64 functions, 4 injective
options.explanation: 4 is "4 choose 3", the number of possible sets of 3 outputs. Each such set can be hit in 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 orders, so there are 4 × 6 = 24 injections.

questions.workedExample:
**All functions.** A function is a choice of output for each input, independently. Each of the 3 inputs has 4 choices:

```formula
N_all = n^m
N_all = 4 × 4 × 4 = 4^3 = 64
where
N_all: the number of functions from A to B
n: the number of elements of B (possible outputs), 4
m: the number of elements of A (inputs), 3
n^m: m copies of n multiplied together
In words: 3 independent choices from 4 outputs give 64 functions.
```

**Injections.** Outputs must be distinct, so each choice removes one option: 4 for the first input, 3 for the second (not the first output), 2 for the third.

```formula
N_inj = n! / (n − m)!
N_inj = 4! / 1! = 4 × 3 × 2 = 24
where
N_inj: the number of injective functions from A to B
n: the number of possible outputs, 4
m: the number of inputs, 3
!: factorial: the product of every whole number from 1 up to that number, so 4! = 24 and 1! = 1
In words: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 of the 64 functions never repeat an output.
```

Check with Python:

```python
from itertools import product
fs = list(product(range(4), repeat=3))
len(fs)                           # 64
sum(len(set(f)) == 3 for f in fs)  # 24
```

questions.prompt: Select all the statements that are true. Here ∅ is the empty set, ∈ means "is an element of", ⊆ means "is a subset of", and vertical bars around a set mean its number of elements.

options.explanation: True. The empty set is a subset of every set, because it has no element that could fail to be in {1, 2}.
False. ∈ asks whether ∅ is one of the listed elements. The elements are 1 and 2; ∅ is not among them.
True. {∅} is a set whose single element is the empty set. Confusing {∅} with ∅ is the classic mistake.
True. Sets ignore order and repetition, so both have exactly the elements 1 and 2.
False. {1} ⊆ {1, 2} is true, but the elements of {1, 2} are the numbers 1 and 2, not the set {1}.

questions.workedExample:
Separate *is an element of* (∈) from *is a subset of* (⊆).

```formula
∅ ⊆ {1, 2}
∅ ∉ {1, 2}
|{∅}| = 1
{1, 2} = {2, 1, 1}
{1} ⊆ {1, 2}
{1} ∉ {1, 2}
where
∅: the empty set, with no elements
⊆: is a subset of: every element on the left is also on the right
∈: is an element of
∉: is not an element of
| |: the cardinality: the number of elements
{ }: the set of the things listed inside
=: the sets have exactly the same elements
In words: every line here is a true fact. The empty set is a subset of everything but is not listed in {1, 2}, so option B is false; {∅} has one element; order and repeats don't change a set; and {1} is a subset of {1, 2} but not one of its elements, so option E is false.
```

1. The empty set is a subset of every set: the statement "every element of ∅ is in the set" has no counterexample.
2. ∅ ∈ {1, 2} would need ∅ to be listed inside the braces. It isn't.
3. {∅} contains one thing, the empty set, so its cardinality is 1. Compare `len([[]])` in Python, which is 1.
4. Set equality only depends on membership, so {2, 1, 1} = {1, 2}.
5. {1} is a set, and {1, 2} contains numbers, so {1} is not an element of {1, 2} even though it is a subset.

questions.prompt: A colleague wants a hash function from 64-bit account numbers to 32-bit slot numbers in a table that is guaranteed to have no collisions for any possible input. What is the right response?

options.text: Use a cryptographic hash such as SHA-256 truncated to 32 bits
options.explanation: Truncation cannot remove the pigeonhole limit. A 32-bit output is also too small for cryptographic collision resistance: generic birthday search needs only about 2¹⁶ trials.

options.text: It is impossible: no injective function exists from a 2⁶⁴-element set to a 2³²-element set
options.explanation: Correct. An injection can exist only when the domain is no larger than the codomain. With 2⁶⁴ inputs and 2³² outputs, the pigeonhole principle forces collisions, so the table must handle them.

options.text: Use the ID mod 2³² as the slot
options.explanation: Taking the remainder after dividing by 2³² keeps only the low 32 bits. IDs that differ only in the high bits, like 1 and 2³² + 1, collide.

options.text: It is possible if the function is a bijection
options.explanation: A bijection needs equal-sized sets. 2⁶⁴ is not equal to 2³², so no bijection (or injection) exists.

questions.workedExample:
Frame it as a question about functions between finite sets.

```formula
|A| = 2^64   |B| = 2^32
|A| = 2^32 × |B|
|A| > |B|
where
A: the domain: every possible 64-bit account number
B: the codomain: every 32-bit slot number in the table
| |: the cardinality: the number of elements
2^64, 2^32: 64 or 32 copies of 2 multiplied together: the number of different 64-bit and 32-bit values
>: is greater than
In words: there are 2^32 (about 4.3 billion) times as many IDs as slots, so an injection, which needs |A| ≤ |B|, cannot exist.
```

By pigeonhole, some slot must receive at least 2³² IDs.

What *is* achievable: if you only ever store a known, fixed set of at most 2³² IDs, a **perfect hash function** for that particular set can avoid collisions. But "for any possible input" rules that out. General-purpose hash tables need a collision policy, such as chaining or probing; a table tailored to a fixed key set can instead use perfect hashing.

questions.prompt:
What does this print?

```python
n = 5
c = 0
for m in range(1 << n):
    if bin(m).count('1') == 2:
        c += 1
print(c)
```

options.explanation: 32 is the number of masks the loop visits (all subsets). The `if` filters to masks with exactly two bits set.
20 is 5 × 4, which counts *ordered* pairs of distinct positions. A bitmask has no order, so each pair is counted twice: 20 / 2 = 10.
25 is 5², which would count ordered pairs allowing repeats. A mask cannot set the same bit twice.
Correct. Masks with exactly two 1-bits among 5 positions correspond to 2-element subsets of a 5-element set, and there are "5 choose 2" = 10 of them.

questions.workedExample:
1. `1 << 5` is 32, so `m` runs over 0..31: every subset of {0,1,2,3,4}.
2. `bin(m).count('1')` is the number of elements in the subset.
3. We count subsets of size exactly 2.

List them to be sure:

```
{0,1} {0,2} {0,3} {0,4}
{1,2} {1,3} {1,4}
{2,3} {2,4}
{3,4}
```

That is 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10, which matches the formula for choosing 2 items out of 5:

```formula
C(n, k) = n! / (k! × (n − k)!)
C(5, 2) = (5 × 4) / (2 × 1) = 10
where
C(n, k): "n choose k": the number of k-element subsets of an n-element set
n: the number of bit positions, 5
k: the number of bits set, 2
!: factorial: the product of every whole number from 1 up to that number, so 5! = 120 and 2! = 2
In words: 5 × 4 counts ordered pairs of positions, and dividing by 2 removes the double counting, since a bitmask has no order.
```

questions.prompt: A query filters with `WHERE NOT (country = 'UK' OR plan = 'free')` (assume no NULLs). Which condition selects exactly the same rows?

options.text: `country <> 'UK' AND plan <> 'free'`
options.explanation: Correct. By De Morgan's law, NOT (A OR B) is (NOT A) AND (NOT B). As sets: the complement of the union of UK rows and free rows is the intersection of the non-UK rows and the non-free rows.

options.text: `country <> 'UK' OR plan <> 'free'`
options.explanation: This keeps the OR. De Morgan's law flips OR to AND when you push the NOT inside. This version would include UK users on paid plans.

options.text: `NOT country = 'UK' OR plan = 'free'`
options.explanation: NOT binds tighter than OR, so this is `(country <> 'UK') OR plan = 'free'`, which includes free users, exactly the ones the original excludes.

options.text: `country = 'UK' AND plan = 'free'`
options.explanation: This is the intersection, not the complement of the union. It selects UK free users, who are excluded by the original.

questions.workedExample:
Think of the rows as sets:

```formula
(A ∪ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ
where
U: the universe: every row of the table
A: the rows with country = 'UK'
B: the rows with plan = 'free'
∪: union: rows in A or B (SQL OR)
∩: intersection: rows in both (SQL AND)
ᶜ: complement: the rows of U not in the set (SQL NOT)
In words: rows that are in neither set are exactly the rows that are outside A and also outside B.
```

1. The original keeps (A ∪ B)ᶜ: rows in neither set.
2. Aᶜ is `country <> 'UK'`, Bᶜ is `plan <> 'free'`, and ∩ is AND.

Check with one row per region:

```
UK,free    orig: no   answer: no
UK,paid    orig: no   answer: no
FR,free    orig: no   answer: no
FR,paid    orig: yes  answer: yes
```

The De Morgan rewrite also holds under SQL three-valued logic. With NULLs, UNKNOWN is not the same as FALSE, so a set-complement interpretation of filtered rows needs care.

questions.prompt:
Take two functions and their composition:

```formula
f : A → B,   g : B → C
(g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x))
where
f: a function from the set A to the set B
g: a function from the set B to the set C
A, B, C: sets
x: an input from A
→: in "f : A → B", f takes inputs from A and gives outputs in B
∘: composition: g ∘ f means "apply f, then g"
In words: g ∘ f is the function from A to C that runs f and then feeds the result to g.
```

Suppose g ∘ f is known to be **injective**. Which statements must be true? (|A| means the number of elements of A.)

options.text: f is injective
options.explanation: Must be true. If f sent two different inputs to the same place, g would then send them to the same place too, so g ∘ f would not be injective.

options.text: g is injective
options.explanation: Not necessarily. g only has to be injective on the image of f. It can merge elements of B that f never hits: see the one-element example in the worked example.

options.text: f is surjective
options.explanation: Not necessarily. In the worked example, f never hits q, yet g ∘ f is injective.

options.text: |A| ≤ |C| when the sets are finite
options.explanation: Must be true. g ∘ f is itself an injection from A to C, and an injection between finite sets needs a domain no bigger than its codomain.

questions.workedExample:
Test each claim: prove it, or find a tiny counterexample.

1. **f injective.** Suppose two different inputs collide in f. Applying g keeps them collided:

```formula
f(x) = f(y)   with x ≠ y
g(f(x)) = g(f(y))
where
f: the first function, from A to B
g: the second function, from B to C
x, y: two inputs from A
≠: is not equal to
In words: if f merges x and y, then g ∘ f merges them too, contradicting injectivity of g ∘ f. So f must be injective.
```

2. **g injective.** Counterexample:

```formula
A = {1}   B = {p, q}   C = {z}
f(1) = p
g(p) = z,   g(q) = z
where
A, B, C: tiny example sets
p, q: the two elements of B
z: the only element of C
f: the function from A to B
g: the function from B to C
In words: g merges q with p, but g ∘ f has only one input, so it is trivially injective.
```

3. **f surjective.** The same example: q is never hit.
4. **|A| ≤ |C|.** g ∘ f itself is an injection from A to C, and injections between finite sets never go from bigger to smaller.

The engineering lesson: a lossy early stage cannot be fixed later, but a later stage may be lossy on inputs that never reach it.

questions.prompt: Which of these sets is **uncountable**?

options.text: All finite strings over the alphabet {0, 1}
options.explanation: Countable. List them by length, then alphabetically: the empty string, 0, 1, 00, 01, 10, 11, 000, … Every string appears at some finite position.

options.text: All syntactically valid Python programs
options.explanation: Countable. Each program is a finite string over a finite character set, and a subset of a countable set is countable.

options.text: All functions from ℕ to {0, 1}
options.explanation: Correct. These are infinite binary sequences, and Cantor's diagonal argument shows no list can contain them all.

options.text: The rational numbers ℚ
options.explanation: Countable, surprisingly. Fractions can be listed by walking the grid of (numerator, denominator) pairs diagonally, skipping duplicates such as 2/4.

questions.workedExample:
A set is countable if you can list it as a sequence that reaches every element after finitely many steps.

1. Finite strings: list by length. Countable.
2. Programs are finite strings, so a subset of (1). Countable.
3. Fractions: zig-zag through the grid of (numerator, denominator) pairs. Countable.
4. Functions from ℕ to {0, 1} are infinite bit sequences. Assume a complete list of them and build a new sequence d from the diagonal:

```formula
d(i) = 1 − s_i(i)
where
s_i: the i-th sequence in the supposed list
s_i(i): bit number i of sequence s_i (the diagonal)
d: the new sequence
d(i): bit number i of d
i: a position, 1, 2, 3, …
ℕ: the natural numbers 0, 1, 2, …
In words: each bit of d is the flipped diagonal bit, so d differs from the i-th sequence at position i.
```

```
s1 = 0 1 1 0 ...
s2 = 1 0 0 1 ...
s3 = 1 1 1 0 ...
d  = 1 1 0 ...
```

d differs from every listed sequence somewhere, so it is missing from the list. Uncountable.

Combining (2) and (4): there are more yes/no problems than programs, so some problems cannot be solved by any program.

questions.prompt:
Consider this function:

```formula
f : ℤ → ℕ,   f(x) = x^2
ℕ = {0, 1, 2, …}
where
f: the squaring function
ℤ: the integers …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, … (the domain)
ℕ: the natural numbers, here including 0 (the codomain)
x: an integer input
x^2: x × x
→: in "f : ℤ → ℕ", f takes integers and its declared codomain is ℕ
…: and so on
In words: f squares an integer and is declared to give a natural number.
```

Which is correct?

options.text: Injective, because squaring is one-to-one
options.explanation: On all integers, −3 and 3 both square to 9. Squaring is injective on the non-negative integers, and also on the non-positive integers, but not on all integers.

options.text: Surjective, because every natural number is a square of something
options.explanation: Most natural numbers are not perfect squares. 2, 3, 5, 6, 7 and 8 are never outputs.

options.text: Neither injective nor surjective
options.explanation: Correct. −1 and 1 both square to 1, which breaks injectivity, and 2 has no integer square root, which breaks surjectivity.

options.text: Bijective onto its image, so it has an inverse from ℕ to ℤ
options.explanation: Restricting the codomain to the image {0, 1, 4, 9, …} makes f surjective, but it is still not injective (a number and its negative collide), so f cannot be inverted.

questions.workedExample:
Check both properties with specific values.

1. **Injective?** Look for two inputs with the same output:

```formula
f(−2) = (−2)^2 = 4
f(2) = 2^2 = 4
where
f: the squaring function from the integers to ℕ
ℕ: the natural numbers 0, 1, 2, …
In words: −2 and 2 are different inputs with the same output, so f is not injective.
```

2. **Surjective?** Look for a codomain element nobody hits. The outputs are:

```
input  : -3 -2 -1  0  1  2  3
square :  9  4  1  0  1  4  9
```

2 never appears (no integer squared gives 2). Not surjective.

Note how both properties depend on declared sets: restrict the domain to ℕ and f becomes injective; restrict the codomain to perfect squares and it becomes surjective.

questions.prompt: Assume a deterministic encoder and decoder satisfy `decode(encode(x)) == x` for every valid value x. View `encode` as a total mathematical function from Values to Bytes, and `decode` as one from Bytes to Values, where Bytes is an accepted byte-string domain containing every encoded value. What follows?

options.text: encode is a bijection between values and byte strings
options.explanation: It doesn't force surjectivity: accepted byte strings with non-canonical JSON whitespace, for example, need not be produced by the chosen canonical encoder.

options.text: decode is injective
options.explanation: decode can map several byte strings to the same value, for example JSON with different whitespace. Only encode is forced to be injective.

options.text: encode is injective, and decode is surjective onto Values
options.explanation: Correct. If two values encoded to the same bytes, decode would have to return both of them from one input, so encode is injective. Every value x is what decode returns for encode(x), so decode hits everything.

options.text: encode(decode(b)) == b for every byte string b
options.explanation: That is the reverse round trip, and it fails for non-canonical inputs: decoding `{ "a":1 }` and re-encoding may give `{"a":1}`.

questions.workedExample:
The premise says decode undoes encode:

```formula
decode(encode(x)) = x   for every x
where
encode: the encoder, a function from Values to Bytes
decode: the decoder, a function from Bytes to Values
x: any valid value
In words: encoding then decoding always gives back the original value, so decode ∘ encode is the identity on Values.
```

From that alone:

1. **encode is injective.** Suppose two values give the same bytes:

```formula
encode(x) = encode(y)
x = decode(encode(x))
  = decode(encode(y)) = y
where
encode: the encoder, from Values to Bytes
decode: the decoder, from Bytes to Values
x, y: two valid values
In words: if x and y encode the same way, decoding gives the same answer for both, and that answer is both x and y, so they were the same value.
```

2. **decode is surjective.** For any value x, the byte string encode(x) decodes to x.
3. **Nothing else is forced.** Accepted byte strings outside the image of encode can decode to other valid values; rejected inputs lie outside this total decoder domain, and different byte strings can decode to the same value.

This is a standard result: whenever one function exactly undoes another, the first is injective and the second is surjective. Property-based tests supply evidence on the cases generated; they do not establish the universal premise unless the entire finite domain is exhaustively checked.

lessons.title: Relations, equivalence classes and partial orders
lessons.summary: Binary relations and their properties, equivalence relations and the partitions they create, partial orders, Hasse diagrams, topological sorting and closures.
lessons.body:
A function links each input to exactly one output. A **relation** is the looser idea: any collection of links between things. "Follows" on a social network, "depends on" between packages, "is congruent to mod 7" between integers and "happened before" between events in a distributed system are all relations.

Two special kinds of relation do a huge amount of work in computer science. **Equivalence relations** say when two things count as "the same" and split a set into groups. **Partial orders** say when one thing must come "before" another, and are what a build system or a task scheduler sorts.

## What a relation is

A **binary relation** from a set A to a set B is just a set of ordered pairs: it lists which elements of A are linked to which elements of B. A relation on a single set uses pairs from that set on both sides.

```formula
R ⊆ A × B
a R b   means   (a, b) ∈ R
where
R: the relation, written as the set of linked pairs
A, B: the sets the first and second parts of each pair come from
×: Cartesian product: A × B is the set of every ordered pair whose first part is in A and second part is in B
⊆: is a subset of
a: an element of A
b: an element of B
a R b: infix shorthand, read "a is related to b by R"
( , ): an ordered pair: (a, b) and (b, a) are different
∈: is an element of
In words: a relation is any chosen set of pairs (for a relation on one set A, take B to be A as well). Writing a R b is just a shorter way to say that the pair (a, b) is in the set.
```

For example, "is less than" on {1, 2, 3} is the relation {(1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)}: 1 < 2 holds, so (1, 2) is in it, while 2 < 1 fails, so (2, 1) is not.

Three equivalent pictures of the same relation on {1, 2, 3}:

```
pairs:   {(1,1), (1,2), (2,3)}

matrix:      1  2  3
          1  1  1  0
          2  0  0  1
          3  0  0  0

graph:   1 --> 2 --> 3
         plus a self-loop 1 --> 1
```

The matrix view shows how many relations a set has: every cell is independently 0 or 1.

```formula
N_rel = 2^(n^2)
N_rel = 2^(3^2) = 2^9 = 512   for n = 3
where
N_rel: the number of different relations on the set
n: the number of elements in the set
n^2: n × n, the number of cells in the n-by-n matrix (one per ordered pair)
2^(n^2): 2 multiplied by itself n^2 times: two choices (0 or 1) per cell
In words: a 3-element set has 9 possible ordered pairs, each either in or out, so 2^9 = 512 relations.
```

The count explodes quickly: a 4-element set has 16 possible pairs and already 65,536 relations (16 copies of 2 multiplied together). The graph view is why so much of graph theory is really about relations.

## The four key properties

For a relation R on a set A:

| Property | Definition |
|---|---|
| Reflexive | every element is related to itself |
| Symmetric | every link has its reverse link |
| Antisymmetric | two distinct elements are never linked both ways |
| Transitive | links chain: two steps imply a direct link |

In symbols, one line per row of the table:

```formula
a R a   for every a ∈ A
a R b   ⇒   b R a
a R b and b R a   ⇒   a = b
a R b and b R c   ⇒   a R c
where
R: the relation, a set of pairs from A
A: the set the relation is on
a, b, c: any elements of A (each line must hold for every choice)
a R b: a is related to b, that is, (a, b) is in R
∈: is an element of
⇒: implies: whenever the left side holds, the right side must hold too
In words: reflexive means everything relates to itself; symmetric means links go both ways; antisymmetric means the only way to have links both ways is between an element and itself; transitive means a two-step chain always has a direct link.
```

Test them on "less than or equal to" over {1, 2, 3}: 2 ≤ 2 (reflexive holds), 1 ≤ 2 but not 2 ≤ 1 (symmetric fails), and 1 ≤ 2 and 2 ≤ 3 give 1 ≤ 3 (transitive holds).

In the matrix: reflexive means the diagonal is all 1s, symmetric means the matrix equals its transpose. In the graph: reflexive means a self-loop on every node, symmetric means every edge has a reverse edge, transitive means every two-step path has a shortcut edge.

> [!warning] Antisymmetric is not "not symmetric"
> Antisymmetric only forbids two-way links between *different* elements. Equality (=) is both symmetric and antisymmetric. The relation {(1, 2), (2, 1), (1, 3)} is neither: (1, 2) has a reverse, but (1, 3) doesn't.

Some everyday examples:

- **≤ on integers**: reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive. Not symmetric.
- **< on integers**: not reflexive (irreflexive), antisymmetric (vacuously), transitive.
- **"Is a friend of"**: symmetric, usually not transitive.
- **"Follows" on a social network**: none of the four in general.

## Equivalence relations

A relation that is **reflexive, symmetric and transitive** is an **equivalence relation**. It formalises "the same in the way we care about".

Examples:

- **Congruence modulo n**: two integers are related when they leave the same remainder after division by n (see below). Mod 3 groups integers by remainder.
- **Same connected component** in an undirected graph.
- **Case-insensitive equality** of strings: "Hello" and "HELLO" are equivalent.
- **Same hash bucket**: two keys are related when the hash function sends them to the same value. Any relation of the form "same output of some function" is an equivalence relation.

The first and last examples in symbols:

```formula
a ≡ b (mod n)   means   n | (a − b)
17 − 5 = 12 = 4 × 3
so   17 ≡ 5 (mod 3)
x ~ y   means   f(x) = f(y)
where
a, b: integers
n: the modulus, a positive integer (3 in the example)
≡: is congruent to: the two numbers leave the same remainder after division by n
mod: modulo: names the number n we divide by
|: divides: n | m means m is a whole-number multiple of n
x, y: any two elements, such as two hash keys
~: is equivalent to (the relation being defined)
f: any function, such as a hash function h or "birth month"
f(x): the output of f for input x
In words: a and b are congruent mod n when their difference is a multiple of n; 17 and 5 both leave remainder 2 when divided by 3. In general, "x and y give the same output" is always reflexive, symmetric and transitive, because equality of outputs is.
```

The **equivalence class** of an element is everything equivalent to it:

```formula
[a] = { x ∈ A : x ~ a }
where
[a]: the equivalence class of a
a: an element of the set A
A: the set the relation is on
x: a stand-in for each element of A
~: the equivalence relation
∈: is an element of
{ x ∈ A : … }: the set of all x in A that make the condition after the colon true
In words: the class of a collects every element equivalent to a, including a itself.
```

The crucial theorem: **the equivalence classes partition the set**. Every element is in exactly one class, and two classes are either identical or disjoint.

For congruence mod 3, the integers split into three classes:

```formula
[0] = {…, −3, 0, 3, 6, …}
[1] = {…, −2, 1, 4, 7, …}
[2] = {…, −1, 2, 5, 8, …}
where
[0], [1], [2]: the equivalence classes of 0, 1 and 2 under congruence mod 3: the integers leaving remainder 0, 1 and 2 when divided by 3
{ }: the set of the things listed inside
…: and so on without end, in both directions
In words: every integer lands in exactly one of three classes by its remainder mod 3. Negative numbers follow the same pattern: −2 = −1 × 3 + 1, so −2 is in [1].
```

The converse holds too: any partition defines an equivalence relation ("in the same block"). So the number of equivalence relations on an n-element set equals the number of partitions, the **Bell number**: 1, 1, 2, 5, 15, 52, … for sets of 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 elements. For example, {a, b, c} has 5 partitions: everything together, the three ways to pair two elements and leave one alone, and all three apart.

### Equivalence relations in code

The **union-find** (disjoint-set) data structure maintains an equivalence relation as you add facts like "a ~ b". Each class is a tree with a representative at the root. Because the relation is transitive, merging two classes is all you ever need to do.

```python
parent = {}

def find(x):
    parent.setdefault(x, x)
    while parent[x] != x:
        parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
        x = parent[x]
    return x

def union(a, b):
    parent[find(a)] = find(b)

union('a', 'b'); union('b', 'c')
find('a') == find('c')   # True
```

Union-find tracks components for Kruskal's algorithm and can support type-variable unification. Full type unification also needs to handle type structure and checks such as the occurs check.

Python's own contract relies on this theory. Well-behaved value equality is normally an equivalence relation, but Python does not enforce these laws and NaN is a standard exception. Hashable objects that compare equal must have equal hashes, and their hash must stay stable while used as keys.

> [!warning] "Approximately equal" is not an equivalence
> Calling two numbers equal when they are within a small tolerance of each other breaks transitivity, so it cannot be used to bucket values into consistent groups. The example below shows the chain that fails.

```formula
x ~ y   means   |x − y| < 0.1
|0.0 − 0.08| = 0.08   so 0.0 ~ 0.08
|0.08 − 0.16| = 0.08   so 0.08 ~ 0.16
|0.0 − 0.16| = 0.16   so 0.0 ≁ 0.16
where
x, y: any two real numbers
~: "approximately equal", the relation being tested
≁: is not related by ~
| |: around a number, the absolute value: its size ignoring the sign, so |x − y| is the distance between x and y
<: is less than
In words: 0.0 is close to 0.08, and 0.08 is close to 0.16, but 0.0 is not close to 0.16, so the relation is not transitive.
```

## Partial orders

A relation that is **reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive** is a **partial order**. A set with a partial order is a **poset** (partially ordered set). A generic partial order is written with a curly less-than sign:

```formula
a ≼ a
a ≼ b and b ≼ a   ⇒   a = b
a ≼ b and b ≼ c   ⇒   a ≼ c
where
≼: a partial order, read "precedes or equals" or "is below or equal to"
a, b, c: any elements of the set
⇒: implies: whenever the left side holds, the right side must too
In words: everything is below or equal to itself, two different things can't each be below the other, and "below" chains.
```

Examples:

- ≤ on numbers.
- ⊆ on the subsets of a set.
- "Divides" on positive integers (see below).
- "Must be built before" on build targets (taking the reflexive closure).
- "Happened before" on events in a distributed system (Lamport's relation, as a strict order).

Divisibility is worth writing out, because it is the standard example of an order that is not total:

```formula
a | b   means   b = k × a   for some k ∈ ℤ
12 = 4 × 3   so   3 | 12
2 ∤ 3   and   3 ∤ 2
where
|: divides: a | b means b is a whole-number multiple of a
∤: does not divide
a, b: positive integers
k: a whole number, the multiplier
ℤ: the integers …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …
∈: is an element of
In words: a divides b when b is a whole number of copies of a. 3 divides 12, but neither of 2 and 3 divides the other.
```

"Partial" means some pairs may be **incomparable**:

```formula
a ∥ b   means   not a ≼ b and not b ≼ a
{1} ∥ {2}   with ⊆
2 ∥ 3   with |
where
a, b: elements of a poset
∥: is incomparable with
≼: the partial order (here ⊆ or |)
⊆: is a subset of
|: divides
{ }: the set of the things listed inside
In words: two elements are incomparable when neither is below the other. {1} and {2} are not subsets of each other, and neither of 2 and 3 divides the other.
```

If every pair is comparable, it is a **total order** (or linear order), like ≤ on integers or alphabetical order on strings.

A **strict** partial order is irreflexive (nothing is related to itself) and transitive. You get one from a partial order by removing the diagonal, the pairs of each element with itself:

```formula
a ≺ b   means   a ≼ b and a ≠ b
where
≺: the strict order: "is strictly below"
≼: the partial order: "is below or equal to"
a, b: elements of the set
≠: is not equal to
In words: a is strictly below b when it is below or equal to b but not equal to it, just as < is ≤ without the equal case.
```

An acyclic direct-dependency graph need not itself be transitive; its positive-length reachability relation is a strict partial order.

### Hasse diagrams

A **Hasse diagram** draws a poset without clutter: leave out self-loops and any edge implied by transitivity, and put larger elements higher. Here is "divides" on the divisors of 12:

```
        12
       /  \
      4    6
      |  /  \
      2      3
       \    /
        \  /
         1
```

Read upwards: 2 divides 4, and 4 divides 12, so a path upwards means "divides". 4 and 6 are incomparable (no upward path joins them), as are 4 and 3.

Vocabulary that comes up in interviews and papers:

- **Minimal** element: nothing is strictly below it. **Least** (minimum) element: below everything. A poset can have several minimal elements but at most one least element.
- **Chain**: a set of pairwise comparable elements. **Antichain**: pairwise incomparable.
- **Upper bound (order theory)** and **least upper bound (join)**. In the subset order, the join of two sets is their union. Posets where every pair has a join and a meet are **lattices**; state-based CRDTs use a join operation on a semilattice of states; operation-based CRDTs use different delivery and commutativity conditions.

### Topological sorting

A **linear extension** of a poset is a total order that respects it: a list of all the elements in which everything strictly below another element comes earlier.

```formula
a ≺ b   ⇒   pos(a) < pos(b)
where
a, b: elements of the poset
≺: is strictly below in the partial order (for a build: is a prerequisite of)
⇒: implies
pos: the position of an element in the chosen list (1 for first, 2 for second, …)
<: is less than
In words: a valid order never lists something before one of its prerequisites. Elements with no order between them can go either way round.
```

For a finite DAG, finding one is **topological sorting**, and it exists precisely because there are no cycles (a cycle of distinct vertices conflicts with antisymmetry of reachability, and a self-loop would need a target to come strictly before itself).

```python
from graphlib import TopologicalSorter

# target: its prerequisites
deps = {
    'app': {'lib', 'config'},
    'lib': {'utils'},
    'config': set(),
    'utils': set(),
}
ts = TopologicalSorter(deps)
print(list(ts.static_order()))
# e.g. ['config', 'utils', 'lib', 'app']
```

There are usually many valid orders: the incomparable elements can come in any relative order. Build and dependency tools use dependency ordering when prerequisites form a DAG. Cycle policies vary: pip documents an installation fallback for dependency cycles, so not every such tool rejects them.

> [!example] Vector clocks are a partial order
> In a store that tracks versions with vector clocks, each version carries a list of counters, one for each tracked participant. One version is below another when none of its counters is larger. Two versions where neither is below the other are **concurrent**: incomparable in the partial order. Riak and Dynamo-style stores surface these as siblings for the application to merge.

```formula
V ≤ W   means   V_i ≤ W_i   for every i
[2, 1, 0] ≤ [2, 2, 1]
[2, 1, 0] ∥ [1, 2, 0]
where
V, W: two vector clocks: lists of counters, one per participant
V_i, W_i: counter number i in V and in W
i: a position in the list, one per participant
≤: on the left, the order on whole clocks; on the right, ordinary "less than or equal to" on two counters
∥: is incomparable with (concurrent)
[ ]: a vector clock written as its list of counters
In words: one clock is below another when it is behind or level on every counter. [2, 1, 0] and [1, 2, 0] each lead on one counter, so neither is below the other: the two versions were written concurrently.
```

## Closures

Often you have a relation that is "almost" what you want. The **transitive closure** is the smallest transitive relation containing it: it links a to b whenever a chain of one or more links leads from a to b.

```formula
a R⁺ b   means   a R x_1 R x_2 … R x_k R b
1 R 2 and 2 R 3   so   1 R⁺ 3
where
R: the original relation
R⁺: the transitive closure of R, read "R plus"
a, b: elements of the set
x_1, x_2, x_k: the intermediate elements on the chain
k: the number of intermediate steps, which can be 0 (then a R b directly)
…: and so on along the chain
In words: R⁺ adds a direct link for every path of length one or more in R. If 1 links to 2 and 2 links to 3, the closure links 1 to 3.
```

"Can user A reach user B through follows?" and "does package X depend on Y, directly or indirectly?" are transitive-closure questions.

Two standard ways to compute it, viewing the relation as a directed graph:

```formula
T_W = O(n^3)
T_S = O(n × (n + m))
where
T_W: running time of Warshall's algorithm, which works on the adjacency matrix
T_S: running time of a breadth-first or depth-first search (BFS or DFS) from every vertex, using adjacency lists
n: the number of elements (vertices)
m: the number of related pairs (edges)
O( ): big-O: grows no faster than the expression inside, up to a constant factor
In words: Warshall's algorithm costs about n^3 steps whatever the relation looks like; a search from every vertex costs about n searches of n + m steps each.
```

For a sparse relation with 10,000 vertices and 50,000 edges, cubing 10,000 gives a trillion steps while 10,000 × 60,000 is 600 million, so the searches win on the asymptotic bound. That is not a promise of a fixed wall-clock speedup, since constant factors and memory access patterns differ. SQL computes reachability with a recursive CTE.

The **reflexive closure** adds the diagonal, the **symmetric closure** adds reverse edges. The reflexive, symmetric, transitive closure of any relation is an equivalence relation: it groups vertices into connected components after ignoring any edge directions.

## Pitfalls

- **Inconsistent comparators.** Sorting assumes a total (pre)order. A comparator that isn't transitive (say, rock-paper-scissors, or one that compares floats with NaN) can make sort output depend on the input order, or make Java's `TimSort` throw "Comparison method violates its general contract!".
- **NaN breaks reflexivity.** `float('nan') == float('nan')` is `False`, so IEEE 754 floats are not an equivalence relation under `==`. For ordinary float-NaN lookups, retaining the identical key object permits retrieval even though NaN is not equal to itself; another separately created float NaN does not match it.
- **Assuming a total order where only a partial one exists.** Wall-clock timestamps can tie and need not match causality. Lamport timestamps respect causal order but do not detect concurrency; a process-ID tie-breaker can make them total. Vector clocks can expose concurrency under their model.

## Key takeaways
- A relation on a set is any set of ordered pairs of its elements; matrices and directed graphs are two views of the same thing.
- Equivalence relations (reflexive, symmetric, transitive) partition a set into disjoint classes; union-find maintains them incrementally.
- Partial orders (reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive) allow incomparable elements; total orders don't.
- A topological sort is a linear extension of a partial order, and exists exactly when the dependency graph has no cycles.
- Equality, hashing and sorting in real code silently assume these properties; NaN, tolerances and bad comparators break them.

Write "divides" precisely, then check each property.

```formula
a | b  means  b = k × a,  k ∈ ℤ
a = 1 × a   so   a | a
6 = 3 × 2   so   2 | 6
6 ∤ 2
b = k × a,  c = m × b
so   c = (m × k) × a   and   a | c
where
|: divides: a | b means b is a whole-number multiple of a
∤: does not divide
a, b, c: positive integers
k, m: whole-number multipliers
ℤ: the integers …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …
```
